title: Polydextrose: What It Is, Why It Is Used as Fiber, and What It Can Do in the Gut

seo.title: Polydextrose: What It Is, Fiber Uses, and Digestive Effects
seo.meta_description: Polydextrose is a highly branched, poorly digested glucose polymer used as soluble fiber and a bulking ingredient to replace some sugar or fat. It ferments relatively slowly in the colon and can support bowel function, although high intakes can cause gas or laxative effects.
seo.search_intent: Understand what polydextrose is, why it counts as fiber, how manufacturers use it, and which gut and tolerance effects can occur.

excerpt: Polydextrose is a highly branched glucose polymer manufactured so human digestive enzymes cannot easily break most of its bonds. It supplies bulk with little sweetness and relatively little energy, making it useful for adding fiber and replacing part of the sugar or fat in bars, desserts, drinks, and lower-calorie foods. In the colon it is fermented relatively slowly and can influence microbial activity and bowel function.
content_html:
Polydextrose is a highly branched, poorly digested glucose polymer used as soluble fiber and as a bulking ingredient. It is manufactured by linking glucose molecules into a complex network containing many bonds that human digestive enzymes cannot efficiently hydrolyze.

The result is an ingredient with very little sweetness, low energy density, and useful physical bulk for replacing part of sugar or fat.

It does not behave like glucose even though glucose is the starting material

Structure and bonding matter more than the original raw material.

Most polydextrose passes through the small intestine without becoming absorbed glucose.

This is why it is treated as a nondigestible carbohydrate and can contribute dietary fiber.

Why food manufacturers use it for bulk

A high-intensity sweetener can replace sweetness but not the physical mass of sugar.

Polydextrose fills part of that structural role without being very sweet, helping formulate bars, chocolate, dairy products, desserts, and drinks with less sugar or fat.

It can also contribute body, moisture control, and texture.

It provides much less energy than sugar

Clinical and regulatory reviews commonly use an energy value around 1 calorie per gram for polydextrose, compared with 4 calories per gram for digestible carbohydrate.

The difference reflects limited direct digestion plus fermentation and excretion.

The calorie value of a finished food still depends on all of its ingredients.

Polydextrose ferments relatively slowly

Its complex structure requires the activity of multiple microbial groups and tends to be broken down more gradually than rapidly fermented fibers such as inulin.

This can distribute fermentation farther along the colon.

Short-chain fatty acids are produced along with variable amounts of gas.

It can change the gut microbiota

A double-blind crossover feeding trial using 8 g/day reported shifts in selected fecal bacterial groups and fermentation metabolites.

This supports the idea that polydextrose is not physiologically inert filler.

It is still not a probiotic because it is a substrate rather than a live microorganism.

It can influence bowel function

Like other fibers, polydextrose increases nondigested material entering the colon and can alter stool water and bulk.

This may support regularity in some people, especially when baseline fiber intake is low.

Response depends on dose, hydration, microbiota, and the rest of the diet.

How much is tolerated?

A review of clinical tolerance studies found polydextrose was generally better tolerated than many poorly absorbed polyols and estimated an average laxative threshold around 90 g/day or 50 g in a single dose.

Those are experimental averages, not recommended intakes.

Sensitive people can experience gas, bloating, or loose stools at much lower doses.

Polydextrose is not the same as inulin

Both can increase fiber and replace some food solids, but their structures and fermentation rates differ.

Inulin tends to ferment more rapidly, while polydextrose is often described as slower and more distributed in its colonic fermentation.

Products combining several added fibers can produce cumulative GI effects.

How to interpret it on a label

Polydextrose often appears in high-fiber, reduced-sugar, or lower-calorie foods, but those claims do not automatically make the entire product nutritionally ideal.

Polydextrose can also help manufacturers reduce sucrose without leaving a large gap in product mass. This is especially useful in bars and desserts where texture depends on solids, not only sweetness.

When it appears alongside inulin, sugar alcohols, or resistant dextrin, gastrointestinal tolerance reflects the combined nondigestible-carbohydrate load rather than polydextrose alone.

That is why two foods containing the same grams of polydextrose can feel very different if one also contains several other fermentable or osmotically active ingredients.

The practical rule: polydextrose is a low-sweetness functional fiber that adds bulk and ferments slowly. It can help increase fiber intake, while large amounts can still cause gastrointestinal symptoms.

faq.question: Is polydextrose fiber?
faq.answer: Yes. It is a poorly digested carbohydrate used as soluble dietary fiber in many foods.

faq.question: Does polydextrose have calories?
faq.answer: It provides much less energy than sugar; values around 1 calorie per gram are commonly used.

faq.question: Can polydextrose cause diarrhea or gas?
faq.answer: Yes. It is generally well tolerated, but high intakes can cause gas, bloating, loose stools, or a laxative effect.
